#1723. Tech Report: Elsinore review: Andrew Scott brings humor and divinity to this profound bio-drama

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Elsinore review: Andrew Scott brings humor and divinity to this profound bio-drama

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I put my faith in art over god and man.
  • According to recent reports, in the dark of a theater, an audience is given a chance to feel seen while not being perceived.
  • According to recent reports, the latest from Andrew Scott stars the critically revered Irish actor as Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor best remembered for Chariots of Fire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m not a religious person. I put my faith in art over god and man. Through creative collaboration, we create something bigger than ourselves, and possibly eternal. In art, we become gods, creating worlds, heroes, and stories that give others hope, agony, and ecstasy.

According to recent reports, in the dark of a theater, an audience is given a chance to feel seen while not being perceived. You don’t need a brave face here. You just need a beating heart. In this way, Elsinore is a religious experience.

According to recent reports, the latest from Andrew Scott stars the critically revered Irish actor as Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor best remembered for Chariots of Fire. However, written by Stephen Beresford, this film focuses on the last play of Charleson's life, when he starred as Hamlet in the National Theater production, while he was dying from AIDS (unbeknownst to the public).

As you might predict, the Shakespearean tragedy about death and regret proves a powerful parallel to the actor's own story. But even as accolades stack up for Scott's performance here, I don't think you can be adequately prepared for what Elsinore truly has in store.

According to recent reports, set a 1989 London, Elsinore plays out at the height of the AIDS crisis. Men around the world are dying at astonishing numbers, while governments largely ignore their plight. The film picks up with Ian well aware of his status, leaning on loved ones who know, and in some cases are afflicted themselves.

Industry observers note that at 40 years old, he's aware that his time is short. So, what will he do with it? Once the opportunity to play Hamlet on England's prestigious stage is presented, he refuses to turn it down even as his doctor (Olivia Colman) tells him the rigors of such an endeavor will only hurt his longevity. To this, Ian proclaims he'd "rather die from Hamlet than AIDS.".

Sources indicate that as dour as the setup sounds, Elsinore is defiantly streaked with joy and laughs. It's a funny movie in the face of death, and rightly so. During a panel at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), Scott — who also produced Elsinore — explained that this humor was essential, because "the great thing about human beings is that we always look for the light." So, it's just honest to have humor even in these places dark and tragic. After all, Shakespeare did it himself. There is humor in Hamlet too.

In Elsinore, some of the film's comedy comes from the world of theater, where significant personalities shine, including a stage door worker who has the ruthless wit of Hamlet's gravedigger. Elsewhere, Billie Piper, who plays Ian's best friend, gossipy casting agent Patsy Pollock, also brings light and levity alongside her onscreen daughter (Sadie Soverall). Through them, Elsinore gives the audience an understanding of Ian beyond his work, as a friend and an uncle who bellows gleefully as he speaks of theater and love. Yet, this isn’t a glowing portrayal.

A subplot about his soured relationship with queer filmmaker Derek Jarman (David Dawson) explores resentment, possible regrets, and the pressure of being an openly queer figure in the world. Essentially, Derek challenges Ian to come out publicly about his sexuality and his diagnosis, calling him a coward if he doesn't. This thread is frustratingly still of great relevance today, as LGBTQ people's bodies are politicized for merely existing. To the credit of Elsinore director Simon Stone, the film's arguments for privacy versus public openness are hotly argued without determining one as right or wrong. Instead, both how these men chose to live, and how they choose to die, is given the space and dignity to be on their own terms.

Recent findings suggest that while critics out of Telluride Film Festival and TIFF have been mixed on the movie itself, Scott is being universally praised for his performance here. There’s no surprise in that. Not only is Scott one of the most mesmerizing actors working in film and theater today, but Elsinore also has a script that gives him plenty to sink his teeth into. Some may say this is a career-best performance for Scott. But such superlatives risk making reviews feel too easily outdated, as from Fleabag to Ripley, All of Us Strangers to Elsinore, Scott keeps delivering outstanding portrayals.

However, I won't take for granted the tactility that Scott brings to Elsinore. Fear of AIDS at this time was so terrible and ignorant that many feared even touching a patient, a point illustrated by a skittish doctor who washes his hands twice after examining Ian's body. Within this context, the holding of a hand, the clutch of a hug, the stroke of a face, carries a heavier, emotional weight. Scott clearly understands the significance. It is not just in how he touches others, but in how he responds to touch. The treasure of that connection rendered onscreen is so profound that you can practically feel it on your own fingertips.

Sources indicate that herein lies the magic of cinema, where what we see and hear becomes so visceral we can practically sense the warmth of an outstretched hand or the smooth chill of Yorick's skull. And in this experience, we are invited, not only to understand Ian's journey, but also to reflect on our own. None of us are getting out alive. So, what do we choose to live for while we can?

Sources indicate that not every moment in Elsinore is as eloquent as these subtle moments of pleasure and pain through touch. In the third act, Stone falters in his faith in the audience, leaning into clichéd montage depicting terminal illness through maudlin visuals. Stone might've trusted in the Bard, as Charleson did to define Ian's exit. There was a version of this movie, perhaps, where we leave him on the stage, allowing his work to speak for him as he'd hoped. Instead, Stone gives us sickly gray scenes of the actor's decay and thunderous body tremors. Then, he frustratingly fumbles the film's final moment with a clumsy and confounding music cue.

Sources indicate that there’s something ironic in this, because within Elsinore, Ian gripes that Chariots of Fire will be most remembered for its score, not his part in it. Yet in the final shot of Ian, Stone chooses to swell Stefan Gregory's score to drown out all other sounds. Here is supposed to be a scene depicting a theater tradition that Ian spoke of with intense reverence, where the ensemble highlights support for an actor by banging collectively on their respective dressing room windows. It's meant to show you are seen, claimed, and loved. And yet, Stone won't let us hear the banging, which might clatter like applause to the very heavens. It's instead a soaring instrumental. In a movie so clearly in love with life and touch, it's so frustrating that Elsinore's final moment misses the opportunity to drive that home with the incredible power of the sound of human hands. Because in the end, it is our striving to connect and find light in the dark that allows us to live through art, past death.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marriage Story stars Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson reunite in writer/director James Gray's Paper Tiger. But don't expect a desperate rehash of Noah Baumbach's divorce drama.

For one thing, Gray is a filmmaker less drawn to such wall-punching theatrics, as evident through films like Two Lovers, Ad Astra, and Armageddon Time. For another, Driver and Johansson are not lovers in this film, though they are in a love triangle of sorts, with Miles Teller at the center.

Gray gives Driver, Johansson, and Teller some unexpected roles, allowing each a place to display their range. But make no mistake, this is Driver's movie.

Industry observers note that set in 1986 Latest York City, Paper Tiger unfurls the story of a Jewish family from Queens that gets on the wrong side of the Russian mob. In a cozy home in Elmhurst, Irwin Pearl (Teller) raises his two sons, Benjamin (Roman Engel) and Scott (Gavin Goudey), with his dedicated housewife Linda (Johansson).

Far from the cocky persona Teller forged through performances in The Spectacular Now, Whiplash, and the Divergent film series, the 39-year-old actor now oozes doofy dad energy. Teller's signature smirk is swapped for an aw-shucks smile, and a patronizing eyebrow raise that insists, "Father knows best." A pair of oversized eyeglasses completes the look; it's is such an evocative detail of the era that the title card reading "1986" might be deemed egregious.

In a recent development, as Irwin, Teller is guileless, relishing every chance to play with his boys or annoy them with dad jokes. Still, he yearns for their respect, and wilts when his eldest huffs they only have "crappy" stuff because Irwin, an educated engineer, isn't bringing home bank like their uncle, Gary (Driver).

It has been revealed that A former NYPD officer turned security consultant with City Hall connections, Gary Pearl is flashy, rich, and successful in a way his younger brother can only envy. He wears tailored suits and a debonair smile. He drives a luxury car, and brings Peter Luger Steak House takeout to family dinner. So, when Gary promises Irwin a business opportunity to make $10,000, his brother is practically drooling at the possibility.

Gary wants to create a consulting firm with Irwin that would advise Russian immigrants who own property alongside the Gowanus Canal on how to meet the city's building codes. The elder brother insists this legit business shouldn't run them afoul of the Russian mob, but an overeager Irwin makes a misstep that puts all of the Pearls at risk.

Industry observers note that at first, Irwin seems the protagonist of Paper Tiger, but Gray's clever script steadily shifts focus to Gary and Linda. Once Irwin has earned the ire of the Russian mafia, it's up to his brother and wife to fix it, because this family man with zero street smarts is incapable. And in this battle to protect Irwin (and the rest of his household), Gary and Linda become unexpected rivals, in part because they deal with Irwin the same way.

Recent findings suggest that paper Tiger becomes a story about the things we can't say to the person we love. Whether because we don't want to hurt them or we want to protect them, some truths are just too terrible to utter. For Gary, he tries to maintain a breezy exterior, promising Irwin he'll work it out with the mob. But in the meantime, thugs creep into the Pearl home and intimidate them by taking Polaroids of the parents and boys, defenseless in their beds. It's only when Irwin finds these pictures that he finally admits to Linda what's going on.

It has been revealed that she's understandably furious, but she's got a substantial secret of her own: a fatal diagnosis she can't bring herself to share. With the mob threatening his life, Gary and Linda are in a similar situation: with an uncertain amount of time left to set Irwin up so he and the boys will be okay. But wife and brother are not allies, and so their paths lead in different directions, while Irwin spirals in impotent looks of his own.

The tragedy of the film is not so much what happens to Irwin's family, but that — as smart as he is — he can't see the troubles mounting before his very eyes.

Gray's ensemble overall is strong. But Driver dominates the film, committing body and soul. The swagger he employs as Gary schmoozes cops and crooks alike is beguiling, recalling James Caan as Sonny Corleone in The Godfather. But in moments when that veneer cracks, Driver's fear is so sparking the screen itself might catch fire. When he reprimands his onscreen brother with love and radiant frustration, he evokes Al Pacino's Michael Corleone, specifically when he kisses the traitor Fredo. The masculinity and the heartache swell to a violent expression of love.

But Gary isn't as direct as Michael, and so Irwin gets to remain smugly self-righteous, unable to recognize his brother's sacrifices for him. Teller is smartly cast in this role. The bravado that carved his career at the start comes into play in the third act as a shield that Irwin carries to distance himself from his own failings. He is a beloved fool whose smile shocks the audience, because it displays his blissful ignorance.

Recent findings suggest that playing the desperate and dying housewife Linda, Johansson is urged by Gray to go into a space of melodrama the cool blonde has rarely tread. Big bouncy curls, thick eyeglasses, and a raspy Queens accent attempt to scrub the movie star glamour from Johansson's appearance. But it is a futile effort. As weary and mumsy as the costuming of housecoats and made-up eye bags tries to make her, the role of Linda might have been better realized by an actress with a mug, not the face of numerous luxury beauty brands. That might have more firmly grounded the Pearl family's blue-collar identity, and by extension, Linda's grit-teeth determination to secure their future. Johansson tries, but her ache and ire ring hollow.

In a recent development, driver's performance recalls '70s gangster cinema, where toxic masculinity roared with a debonair allure. Teller's jolly blend of ego and ignorance makes his '80s dad a believable buffoon. But Johansson's (perhaps impossible to dim) glamour makes Linda feel like she's from a '50s melodrama, so beautiful and so sad! In this context, as grounded as she aims to make Linda, it still feels heightened, a performance of wifely limitations rather than a portrait of them.

Recent findings suggest that still, even with this tonal collision, Paper Tiger is a thoroughly engaging drama. Gray's dialogue shrewdly builds not only characters, but the barriers of what they can and won't share with each other. Like Conclave, Paper Tiger becomes as much about what's talked around as what's talked about. So, with each moment, in words spoken and unspoken, a labyrinth is built, daring the characters to escape it. And rather than calling us to relate to Irwin, the good guy and family man at the film's center, Gray urges us to share in the frustration of those who love him until the bitter end.

In this way, Paper Tiger is a uniquely thrilling and purposefully infuriating family drama. Because as we watch a final moment unfold that is undeniably sweet and tender, we are haunted by what lies beneath it. Gray challenges us to take that trembling awareness home, and look to our own families, lives, and lies.

In a recent development, paper Tiger was reviewed out of the New York Film Festival, where it was the Opening Night selection. The film will open in theaters on Nov. 13, before opening wide Nov. 20. #1720. I Play Rocky review: Can this crowd-pleaser be an Oscar contender?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1547 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

I Play Rocky review: Can this crowd-pleaser be an Oscar contender?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rocky is such a truly iconic film that it's easy to forget its very existence is a miracle.
  • According to recent reports, peter Gamble's screenplay begins with the future Hollywood star going by Mike Stallone (Anthony Ippolito), hitting auditions with his brawny shoulders and distinctive accent, and getting cast as thug #2 if he's lucky.
  • Enter Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb), a smart and dedicated young woman who pushes Mike not only to write the roles he wants to play but to make a mark with his real name, Sylvester Stallone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocky is such a truly iconic film that it's easy to forget its very existence is a miracle. I Play Rocky is the story of how that miracle was built by the blood, sweat, and tears of an unknown actor and aspiring screenwriter named Sylvester Stallone.

According to recent reports, peter Gamble's screenplay begins with the future Hollywood star going by Mike Stallone (Anthony Ippolito), hitting auditions with his brawny shoulders and distinctive accent, and getting cast as thug #2 if he's lucky. At this point, he's living on the streets, finding comfort in a stray puppy he's taken in, and doing some light sex work to keep them both fed. But all he needs to start the path to Rocky is one person to believe in him.

Enter Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb), a smart and dedicated young woman who pushes Mike not only to write the roles he wants to play but to make a mark with his real name, Sylvester Stallone. Together, they move from the cold streets of Newly introduced York to the sunny hills of Los Angeles. He writes out script after script by hand, then she types them up so he can hopefully sell them. When Rocky finally catches the attention of respected producers, it might seem like a happy ending. But there's one catch that Sly lays down: "I play Rocky.".

Stallone, as an unknown, fought tooth and nail to be the center of the movie he dreamed up to make him a star. But at every step, a new challenge presented itself. His underdog story reflects Rocky's — sometimes literally recreating scenes from the Oscar–winning sensation. But as successfully entertaining and heart-warming as I Play Rocky is, will it be able to stand out to the Academy in this year of extraordinary cinema?

In a recent development, well, for starters, director Peter Farrelly previously won over the Academy with Green Book, which scored Best Supporting Actor for Mahershala Ali, Best Original Screenplay (for Farrelly and his co-writers), and Best Picture. That too was a feel-good film inspired by true events. And to its credit, I Play Rocky is less likely to earn the backlash that Green Book did, as it doesn't engage in problematic racial stereotypes.

Recent findings suggest that what I Play Rocky does offer is a cast that absolutely crackles onscreen. Ippolito takes on a difficult role as Stallone, because even a casual movie fan can recognize this A-lister's signature cadence and tone. To his credit, Ippolito is terrific in the role. Not only does his take on Stallone feel familiar, but he also avoids the trap of making it feel like an impression. This becomes clearer when he's tasked with re-enacting classic Rocky scenes, where the physicality of Stallone demands to be even more in sync with the man himself.

Beyond getting the feel of Stallone right, Ippolito has an easy charisma that sparks chemistry with every scene partner, be it his onscreen lover Robb, a pair of bickering producers (P. J. Byrne, Toby Kebbell), his dynamic Rocky co-star Carl Weathers (Stephan James), or his lumbering dog, Butkus. Ippolito's Sly is radiant with life and determination, a screen presence that Stallone brought to Rocky.

And around him, he's bolstered by terrific supporting players. Byrne and Kebbell prove a terrific comedy duo, turning exposition about movie deals into entertainment. Robb shines, despite being in a role that is an achingly cliched Supportive Wife with no complexity. (As presented here, Sasha has no desires beyond what makes Sly happy.) James is electric, an unapologetic scene-stealer who becomes Sly's ally. Tracy Letts is solidly sneering as an antagonistic studio exec, and Jay Duplass is brightly funny as self-proclaimed asshole director John G. Avildsen.

According to recent reports, together, they craft a fish-out-of-water showbiz comedy slash underdog drama that is undeniably rousing and wonderful. So, why won't that be enough for I Play Rocky to be a contender?

On the ground at the Toronto International Film Festival, when I Play Rocky made its World Premiere, the buzz was thunderous and immediate. Following its first screening, the press lined up in a massive theater for the press-and-marketing-screening to see for themselves if this movie could live up to the hype. For those who've never been, that's a tough crowd, almost daring filmmakers to impress them. And adding to the difficulty, this screening was at 8:30 AM on a Sunday, when most sane people would prefer to be in bed. I was in that audience, and frankly dubious I'd enjoy Farrelly's latest, as I tend to think his best film is Dumb & Dumber. (I noted what I said.) To my surprise and delight, I roared with laughter and cheers, as did the hundreds around me. Speculation sparked that this movie would win the festival's audience award, hands down. And the People's Choice Award out of TIFF can often be a bellwether for Oscar success. According to Awards Radar, since 2000, 33 People's Choice winners have gone on to become Best Picture nominees at the Academy Awards, with nine of them winning — including Green Book. But despite the buzz, I Play Rocky didn't win this honor.

Industry observers note that the People's Choice Award went to La Bola Negra, a Spanish drama by directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi that explores queer identity over 85 years in Spain. That film, while extraordinary, is not a crowd-pleaser. It's 159 minutes long, interweaves multiple narratives, and is inspired by four pages of a play written by poet Federico García Lorca before he was assassinated by a fascist government. It's tragic, romantic, and cerebral. And it has all that in common with the International People's Choice winner, Elsinore, which focuses on Scottish actor Ian Charleson's performance of Hamlet as he was dying of AIDS.

In a recent development, where I Play Rocky had brilliant buzz on its debut, it was a runner-up at the end of the festival. And as award season heats up, there's a trend emerging, favoring tragedies over feel-good stories. Another example: TIFF opened with the inspiring docudrama Being Heumann, helmed by Sian Heder, director of the Best Picture winner CODA. While this follow-up has been praised for its representation of people with disabilities in telling the story of disability advocate Judith Heumann, the praise for the movie itself has been muted.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Calvo and Ambrossi are gathering buzz for the Best Director honor, and Andrew Scott seems a frontrunner for his heart-wrenching performance in Elsinore. And then of course, there's the massive wooden horse in the room: The Odyssey.

Recent findings suggest that being both an unadulterated hit with critics and a box office smash that not only brought audiences back to theaters, but also sold out IMAX theaters across the country, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is going to be hard to beat this Oscar season. He brought together a sprawling cast, shot on location, and used practical effects to extraordinary ends to reimagine Homer's Greek epic for a modern, mainstream audience. It is a collision of poetry, craftsmanship, and performance that is absolutely astounding. The Odyssey indicated succinctly why movies still matter, connecting a story that's centuries old to contemporary politics without feeling like it was talking down to its audience.

Sources indicate that there, I Play Rocky falls short. While it is a movie about the importance of cinema, which the Academy loves, it's a look back that feels more a celebration of Stallone than it does a story urgent to now. And in the final act, Farrelly gets carried away in recreating Rocky, pulling in one scene after another to diminishing returns. While his film is still a sensational experience, its final act leans too heavily into the audience's presumed love of Rocky, instead of trusting in their interest of the story being told. And hey, in another year, that might not have been a fatal flaw; it might not even be one that will keep I Play Rocky from some big nominations. But even though I'd argue I Play Rocky is a better movie than Green Book, I wouldn't bet Farrelly's film has a fighting chance against its TIFF peers, much less Nolan's epic.

Industry observers note that I Play Rocky was reviewed out of the Toronto International Film Festival. It opens in limited release in the U.S. and UK on Nov. 6, before going nationwide in the U.S. on Nov. 20. Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard.
  • Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release.
  • So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard. If you're not playing it but are reading this, we can guess why.

Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release. If that's the case, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of the year — and possibly all time. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

Industry observers note that the primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

Recent findings suggest that by all accounts, GTA 6 is a pretty fantastic video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

Recent findings suggest that one thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

Lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing. If you're not sure whether to buy a PS5 or the Xbox Series X/S, keep scrolling for a breakdown of the pros and cons.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

Industry observers note that both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is right now out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

There are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that you won't like the game, though so far, most people who have played it have come away with positive impressions. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the upcoming game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

Maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There was a lot of anxiety on the internet prior to the game's launch surrounding the potential differences between the different console versions. The good news is that the game is out and has been fully tested by experts, and the verdict is that you almost can't go wrong with GTA 6 on any platform.

It has been revealed that digital Foundry is an outlet and YouTube channel that offers expert-level tech analysis of games, and they have a fairly comprehensive guide to the different console versions of GTA 6. According to DF, both the PS5 and Series X versions run at the same resolution and target the same frame rate, with some performance dips on both in more intense sequences. In other words, the base PS5 and Series X versions are roughly the same, though the PS5's controller does have exclusive haptic feedback features for gameplay like driving cars.

There is also the matter of the PS5 Pro and Xbox Series S consoles, though. DF says the PS5 Pro is the best version of the game, with a sharper resolution and higher-quality shadows to go along with smoother performance. That was to be expected. Sadly, it sounds like the Series S version is probably the least desirable build of the game. Its visuals have been marginally downgraded with a lower resolution and some reduced visual settings, but more importantly, DF's analysis found that the frame rate can dip below 20fps in extreme circumstances.

In a recent development, we do have good news for Xbox Series S gamers, however. Mashable Editorial Director Eric Miller has played the game on Series S and has had a positive first impression so far. If you have no other way to play GTA 6, it should work, but it will be reduced in quality compared to the others.

There is technically a way to play GTA 6 without buying a new PS5 or Xbox, but it's not a viable alternative for most people.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

It has been revealed that if game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not stated anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.

AI toys still not ready for primetime

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.
  • The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research.
  • The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research. While some AI products made crucial safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

Recent findings suggest that R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The bunny is at the moment listed on Amazon and available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross remarked, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross said she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three upcoming AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

Sources indicate that in testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

Industry observers note that "Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

Industry observers note that the GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she remarked it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

According to recent reports, in a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

"These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross noted.

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

In a recent development, foloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

The Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester said they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross stated there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

Even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross said.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also said some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

The model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

"We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross noted. "There's a lot of unanswered questions.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.

Sources indicate that the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other. One is the European Space Agency's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO. The other is Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, nicknamed Mio.

A big engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov. 21.

Mercury is the least explored planet in the inner solar system. Only two spacecraft have ever visited it, NASA's Mariner 10 in the 1970s and Messenger in the 2010s. That will make BepiColombo just the second mission to orbit Mercury and the first to put two orbiters there at once. One probe will observe the planet itself and the other will study its space environment. Scientists hope the results will show how rocky planets like Earth form and change when they're born close to their star.

Recent findings suggest that reaching Mercury is actually harder than getting to Pluto. Falling toward the sun isn't the only problem. It's bleeding off enough energy to avoid overshooting the planet.

Industry observers note that bepiColombo launched on Oct. 20, 2018, on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. For most of the trip, it rode on a separate engine module that used ion thrusters. These engines push the spacecraft by firing charged particles out the back. The force was about as strong as the weight of two sheets of paper resting on your hand. But the thrusters ran for two years, carrying the spacecraft about 6 billion miles.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft also used gravity from nearby planets to bend its path. It swung past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times. In Sep. 2024, it passed within about 100 miles of Mercury, the closest any spacecraft has ever flown past a planet. The trip wasn't smooth sailing. The engine module's solar panels started losing power, so the team had to slow down and push back the arrival date. Controllers detached the engine module on Sep. 3.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a very difficult mission and very challenging because we are flying into a very, very harsh environment," Bruno Sousa, ESA's head of operations definition and engineering, noted during a livestream that day. Mercury's surface can drop below -290 degrees Fahrenheit at night and climb above 750 degrees during the day. The spacecraft gets baked from two sides — by sunlight and heat rising off the planet.

Recent findings suggest that the arrival itself is unusual. Most missions hit the brakes hard and drop straight into orbit. BepiColombo is coming in slowly instead, and it gets there in steps. First, it drifts into Mercury's gravitational grip on a loose, irregular path that doesn't loop all the way around the planet. Engineers call this "weak capture." Spacecraft operations manager Ignacio "Nacho" Clérigo said no one has tried it with a planet before, only with moons. Saturday's massive burn swaps that wandering path for a true orbit. It starts out as a long, lopsided oval, and the spacecraft fires its engines about every three days to reel it in.

As the orbit tightens, a series of handoffs follow. On Dec. 9 and 10, the European orbiter releases Mio into its final orbit. Full science work should begin in April 2027.

Mercury holds plenty of puzzles. It's unusually heavy for its size. Apart from Earth, it's the only rocky planet with a magnetic field surrounding the whole planet. Scientists want to learn whether Mercury's huge liquid core has a solid center. Others strategy to measure magnesium, potassium, and calcium in the space around Mercury. Those elements offer indirect clues about what the surface is made of.

It has been revealed that the mission is named for Italian mathematician and engineer Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo. His work on using planets' gravity to steer spacecraft helped make the earlier Mercury missions possible as well as BepiColombo's long, looping route.

Can GTA 6 teach men to be better boyfriends? We asked a relationship therapist.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, since Rockstar released previews of Grand Theft Auto VI this summer, social media has buzzed about the relationship system at the heart of the game.
  • Now that GTA 6 is out, discussion of the latter has resurfaced on X:.
  • But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, since Rockstar released previews of Grand Theft Auto VI this summer, social media has buzzed about the relationship system at the heart of the game. While some critics jumped to say that playing GTA 6 is cheating on your significant other, others speculated that playing the game might actually make players better at IRL connections — especially considering that young adults have less experience.

Now that GTA 6 is out, discussion of the latter has resurfaced on X:.

But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL? To answer that question, I reached out to sex and couples therapist Ilana Grines, whom I previously spoke to about whether playing the game is cheating.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

Sources indicate that "We have to be really careful about what we're claiming that video games can actually do for us," Grines noted. It's useful when individuals are exposed to behaviors that are typically associated with relationship satisfaction as a whole — like spending time together — but, she said, "your girlfriend doesn't have a meter on her forehead that increased the more you...show her attention.".

Recent findings suggest that part of the online conversation stems from the relationship between GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia, whose connection develops through the player's actions. While players can choose to keep their relationship platonic, the game still tracks their bond. Holding hands, buying flowers, giving compliments, sending texts, and running errands together (which may or may not involve committing crimes) can all improve their relationship score.

The relationship meter gives players a sense of where Jason and Lucia stand with one another, Mashable's editorial director Eric Miller explained to me, a self-professed non-gamer. While previous GTA games have featured romantic relationships and family dynamics, GTA 6 takes things a step further by allowing players to actively shape the protagonists' relationship. Depending on their actions, Jason and Lucia can be running on empty (1/4), partners in crime (2/4), crazy in love (3/4), or hot together (4/4).

Grines is skeptical that simply performing these actions in a game can teach emotional intelligence. "You're literally playing a game when you could be participating in your relationship," Grines continued. That's another line of thinking that's echoed on social media today: That people (mostly men) are doing chores for Lucia instead of their IRL girlfriend.

It has been revealed that one of Grines' clients told her that his girlfriend isn't letting him buy the game — but not because of Lucia. It's actually because of the strip club scenes and how realistic the characters look. The girlfriend isn't comfortable with him going to strip clubs in real life, so why would she be comfortable with him going to one in a video game? As in our discussion over whether playing GTA 6 is cheating, Grines mentioned she's entitled to set a boundary.

Real relationships, of course, are more complicated than any in-game relationship meter can capture. And Grines warns against having unrealistic expectations for how video games can improve romance. While seeing a healthy relationship modeled in front of you can be useful, she mentioned that modeling doesn't always create behavioral change. Being a good boyfriend in the game doesn't factor in a real partner's own preferences, emotions, and agency. (For example, your real girlfriend may hate flowers!).

That doesn't mean GTA 6 can't bring couples closer together. Gaming can be a shared experience, as PCMag's Jordan Minor demonstrated when he played the game with his wife.

"It's great that people can experiment and they can repeat actions that may improve their relationship satisfaction," she remarked. "The real test will be if they can take it out of the video game and into their real lives.".

In a recent development, not everyone likes this element of the game. Right-wing (or right-wing adjacent) influencers Asmongold and Clavicular (who was indicted on two rape charges yesterday) expressed their distaste for GTA 6. The former called the game a "cuck simulator" while playing it on stream, and Clavicular mentioned the game is "insanely cucked.".

Then again, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game of all time, so the haters are in the minority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

Recent findings suggest that in September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

Sources indicate that his startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a upcoming class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”.

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

It has been revealed that “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”.

Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”.

Industry observers note that as a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Industry observers note that early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

Recent findings suggest that when Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.

“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he notes.

To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

According to recent reports, in April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

It has been revealed that less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” notes Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”.

Recent findings suggest that seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.”.

In a recent development, when the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.

The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” states Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”.

It has been revealed that by the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”.

Industry observers note that dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

In a recent development, “You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” indicates Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”.

It has been revealed that but Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Massive picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”.

In a recent development, so far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

Recent findings suggest that if he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these fresh missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?

It has been revealed that dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these concerns. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global matter. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he indicates. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”.

But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, introduced a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.

“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he states. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”.

According to recent reports, polemos Industries declared itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first manufacturer. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

In a recent development, dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he says. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”.

#1689. ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Is a Perfect Game. Rushing Through It Would Be a Mistake

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (708 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Is a Perfect Game. Rushing Through It Would Be a Mistake

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club.
  • It has been revealed that the biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best.
  • In a recent development, I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club. Look, I know that’s what you want to do right away when you start Grand Theft Auto VI. This is a GTA game after all—that sort of outlet for titillation is a common theme in this franchise. But going straight to the good stuff isn’t the best way to play this game.

It has been revealed that the biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best. With near-universally perfect review scores, GTA VI has emerged as an absolute behemoth that has lived up to 13 years of hype.

In a recent development, I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn. The GTA franchise has always been high-octane, arcade-style, prioritizing hyperviolence and exaggerated physics that let your character go wild in the digital sandbox. But the latest installation is much more reserved. Vehicles and player movements feel heavier. The characters have deeper, more emotional backstories and motivations. The world has more interactivity and reacts to your actions in much more varied ways.

It evokes a play style that feels very much in common with Rockstar’s previous title, Red Dead Redemption 2. It was a Western that made the player feel the friction of an often slow, plodding life that didn’t shy away from simulating all the chores of a horse-bound cowboy in the 1800s. GTA VI, set in the modern era, is faster-paced but still carries that intentionality to slow the player down.

It has been revealed that that manifests in ways that might feel like busywork. Instead of having access to all your weapons and outfits, you have to make space for the things you want to bring with you and store everything else in the back of your car. You have to call someone to fix your car and wait for them to arrive. Yeah, you have to paint your house and buy your girlfriend flowers. Get used to it. This can sometimes feel like a chore, but it slows the player down to give them time to examine the world around them.

Industry observers note that once you start looking around and really take everything in, the level of detail is truly unique. Leonida—GTA VI’s mirror version of Miami, Florida—is so varied and splendid it is almost overwhelming. After the game’s on-the-rails introductory missions open up into the first opportunity for an open-world sojourn, the sheer scale of this world becomes apparent. Zooming out on the map and seeing the vast expanse of unexplored territory is dizzying.

It has been revealed that there is just so much Leonida, and none of it feels sparse or unfinished. Every place, person, animal, and environmental asset feels fully fleshed out. Driving down the road, with other cars zooming past, is photorealistic enough to look nearly like real dash-cam footage. This game, as I have muttered to myself over and over again while playing, “is simply insane.”.

If you’ve followed the GTA VI saga, this likely won’t surprise you. Developer Rockstar and its parent manufacturer Take-Two have spent around a billion dollars to develop the game. It’s taken 13 years. The company even delayed the game multiple times to make sure it was polished.

There is massive hype, and at this point I’d say what Rockstar has achieved here has surpassed that hype. The game is likely to be the pinnacle of this era of video games, the final grand blockbuster achieved without the use of generative AI.

In a recent development, I’ve been playing GTA games for a long time. I’ll probably be playing this one for the rest of my life. Like me, you’re probably very excited to dive into this gigantic world. The best way to do that is not to try to see it all at once. Pace yourself. Look out for the small moments, as they may lead to something more profound than you’re expecting. Slow down, and you can really feel how the world reacts.

Nothing else like this game exists. And there probably won’t be for a very long time. Might as well make it last.

El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface.
  • The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.
  • A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface. He’s never seen anything like what’s been coming back for the past few months, as a super El Niño fuels record heat off the California coast. The marine heat wave is affecting wildlife and helping to juice the record-setting storms hitting the state at the start of the rainy season.

The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.

A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface. Steric height—changes to sea levels driven by heat rather than melting ice—has reached the highest levels Rudnick has ever seen.

“I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,” Rudnick, who works at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, says.

In Monterey Bay, a station recorded a temperature of 64.72 degrees Fahrenheit (18.18 degrees Celsius) at a depth of 200 feet below the water’s surface in late October, breaking previous records. Other data shows even hotter water in San Diego at the same depth: 77 degrees Fahrenheit, an anomaly of 21.3 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.

It has been revealed that el Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability” off the California coast, Rudnick says. The climate phenomenon is characterized by hotter-than-normal water in the eastern tropical Pacific and affects weather and oceans around the globe. His gliders have captured temperature anomalies across other events, including intense heat during the 2015–2016 super El Niño. But this year’s El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, and its impacts are equally supersized.

“It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,” he says.

According to recent reports, this year’s El Niño is adding heat to an already-simmering ocean. Since January 2025, coastal California waters have been hit by a massive heat wave, with temperatures in some places reaching 8 degrees Fahrenheit above average in August. Add in human-caused climate change—oceans off Southern California have warmed 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s alone—and it makes for unprecedented conditions now.

Industry observers note that “This is a bunch of things that have had to come together to make this even physically possible,” Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, states. “And even then, it's kind of astonishing.”.

Industry observers note that rudnick agrees. “The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,” he says.

Part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures and sea levels off California are what’s known as Kelvin waves. These slow, large waves transport warm water from west to east across the Pacific. They in turn push down the ocean’s thermocline, a transition layer into the deeper ocean where temperatures begin to decrease rapidly.

“It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,” Swain says. “It's just that we've turned off the air conditioner and we're allowing the surface waters to warm.”.

Industry observers note that kelvin waves can also help to raise sea levels along the California coast by “keeping the water from moving physically offshore,” Swain indicates. While Kelvin waves are imperceptible to the average person, their impacts aren’t.

Californians have been living through several weeks of intense coastal flooding and significant waves enhanced by these higher sea levels. San Francisco and the surrounding area are under a coastal flood advisory through Friday morning, and waves have reached over 30 feet (9 meters) in height and even set off seismographs. (Another storm is set to hit the Bay Area this weekend.) It’s also contributing to heavier rainfall, with locations from San Francisco to Burbank setting hourly rainfall records in recent days.

But the warmer water itself is also contributing to this temporary sea level rise, thanks to simple physics: Warmer water takes up more space, helping push up sea levels.

Recent findings suggest that the warm water is driving weather even more unprecedented than the intense storms. On Tuesday, two rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay, the result of cold storm air moving over unusually warm waters. These phenomena are generally seen off the coast of Florida or the Mediterranean—not in the usually frigid waters of the Pacific.

“The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,” Swain says. “It’s an indicator that things aren’t as they usually are in this part of the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that oura has a lock on the world of smart rings, and we've been loving the latest model, which came out this July. Because the Ring 5 is smaller and more comfortable than before, WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane says she often forgets she's even wearing it. In a recent development, we already have smart speakers. We have iPads. We have digital photo frames (or, at least, your parents do). So, a dedicated device that serves merely as a digital calendar might seem superfluous. Maybe it is, but reviewer Nena Farrell absolutely swears by them. It's not just a list of events, either. It also has a meals page to strategy and organize family dinners, plus tasks to keep everyone on top of chores. And this latest 15-inch model, the Skylight Calendar 2, is the best so far.

It's not only our favorite Keychron keyboard—it's the best overall keyboard you can buy. Launched in early 2026, this mechanical keyboard has a mid-century modern vibe, made of wood and metal. The 75 percent layout gives you everything you'll likely need in a compact size, with all the usual Keychron features, such as hot-swappable switches, double-shot keycaps, and the usual excellent build quality. Unlike other mechanical keyboards you may have tried, this one is low-profile, which means the travel distance on each key isn't quite as long, and it's designed for typing first and foremost. It's a great office companion, and it'll be a smoother transition if you're coming from a more generic rubber-dome model like an Apple Magic Keyboard.

The iPhone Duo might be the talk of the town, but the new iPad Mini is the more practical purchase. First of all, it doesn't require trading in the iPhone you're already familiar with to risk it on a first-generation product. It's been almost three years since Apple updated its noise-canceling earbuds, and the latest model adds a newly introduced ear tip design, supports real-time translation, and delivers vastly improved noise canceling and longer battery life. GoPro has a fresh premium camera, and it's one of the most expensive action cameras you can buy. But our camera expert and outdoors enthusiast, Scott Gilbertson, says it's totally worth it. The older GoPro Hero 13 Black is still a great option if you want to save some money, but the Mission 1 Pro's upgrade in image quality is noteworthy for a camera this small.

You can probably imagine how all this tech plays out in a set as immersive as the Star Wars Throne Room Duel. #1683. Breaking: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely.
  • The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one.
  • “Even if you're not a CEO or at a major tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson indicates, because he was “super worried about spies.”.

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.

“Even if you're not a CEO or at a major tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.

One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

Recent findings suggest that “Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One tech giant is pitching its fresh line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” indicates Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”.

Sources indicate that amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking organization Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), claims that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”.

Sources indicate that fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.

The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.

To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she notes, is “a mind fuck.”.

According to recent reports, honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” states Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection organization Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.

The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

Industry observers note that when tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”.

Industry observers note that that setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he notes. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

In a recent development, catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).

For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI introduced a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where users can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.

It made sense, she claims, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin states, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.).

It has been revealed that high-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, says Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.

“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the company and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler says.

According to recent reports, it’s particularly difficult, claims Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

“Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey says. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”.
